To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the self-force on dislocation loops is a complex function of the loop shape, orientation and the anisotropic elastic properties of the material.
the self-forces on dislocation segments depend on the orientation of the dislocation, and on the orientation of a reference frame with respect to the crystal.

the anisotropic self-force on a dislocation segment can be written in terms of the elastic constants and the segment orientation, and that it can be decomposed into a 'core' term that is independent of the crystal orientation, plus a 'lattice' term that is orientation dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of anisotropy in dislocation dynamics.
the study of dislocation motion in anisotropic materials.
the fundamental physics and mechanics of plastic deformation, and the application of this knowledge to understanding and predicting the behaviour of materials under extreme conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self-force on a dislocation segment in an anisotropic crystal is the sum of two terms.
the dislocation self-force in anisotropic crystal is not the same as in isotropic crystal.
the dislocation line tension in anisotropic materials can be anisotropic, and the anisotropic dislocation line tension can be different from the dislocation self-force.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the anisotropy in the dislocation self-force can be significant and that the dislocation self-rotation can be strongly influenced by the anisotropies in elastic constants and in the dislocation core energy.
the self-forces are not negligible, and that their effects are not always intuitive.
the self-force is not simply a couple acting to align the Burgers vector with the dislocation line.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the anisotropy of a dislocation segment can be characterized in terms of its 'energy anisotropy' and 'force anisotropy', the former being the ratio of the segment's minimum energy to its average energy, and the latter being the ratio of its minimum energy to the energy of the pure-screw orientation, in a given crystal orientation.

, while the self-force on a segment of dislocation in an isotropic crystal is a couple that acts to rotate the segment, the self-force on such a segment in an anisotropic crystal can have both a couple and a force component that acts along the dislocation line.
the self-forces on a given dislocation segment depend strongly on the orientations of neighbouring dislocations in the network.
